Correct arguments for the storage account
Explains the plan/apply workflow

questions.title: Debugging a WHERE = NULL mistake
questions.prompt: A junior developer writes WHERE MiddleName = NULL to find customers with no middle name recorded, and gets zero rows back — even though many customers genuinely have a NULL MiddleName. What's actually wrong with that query, and how should they fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: NULL represents an unknown or not-applicable value, not zero or an empty string. Because it's unknown, NULL can't be said to equal anything — not even another NULL — so any comparison using the = operator against NULL evaluates to unknown (treated as false), never true. That means WHERE MiddleName = NULL will always return zero rows, regardless of how many rows actually have a NULL MiddleName, because the comparison can never succeed. The fix is to use the special IS NULL syntax instead: WHERE MiddleName IS NULL. IS NULL isn't a comparison operator — it's dedicated syntax built specifically to test for the absence of a value, and it works correctly where = cannot. The same logic applies to IS NOT NULL for the opposite case.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd point out is that this isn't a typo or syntax error — the query runs fine, it just silently returns the wrong answer, which is the dangerous kind of bug. I'd explain that NULL means 'unknown,' and you can't compare an unknown value to anything using = and expect a meaningful true or false — SQL Server treats that comparison as unknown, which gets filtered out just like false. So WHERE MiddleName = NULL isn't matching NULLs, it's failing to match anything at all. The fix is WHERE MiddleName IS NULL, which is purpose-built syntax for exactly this case rather than a regular comparison. If the goal were actually to display something readable instead of filtering, I'd reach for ISNULL(MiddleName, '(none)') or COALESCE for more than two fallback values.
commonMistakes: Not realizing the query runs without error and silently returns the wrong result, rather than throwing an obvious failure
Treating NULL as if it were an empty string or zero instead of 'unknown'
Using = NULL or <> NULL anywhere instead of IS NULL / IS NOT NULL
Confusing ISNULL() (replaces a NULL with a default, two arguments) with IS NULL (tests for NULL)
keyPoints: NULL means unknown/not applicable, not zero or empty string
= NULL always evaluates to unknown/false, never true
IS NULL / IS NOT NULL is the only correct way to test for NULL
ISNULL()/COALESCE() substitute a default value rather than test for NULL

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses why = NULL fails silently
Provides the correct fix (IS NULL)
Mentions ISNULL/COALESCE as a related but different tool

questions.title: Diagnosing an accidental Cartesian product
questions.prompt: A query joining a 500-row Products table to a 100,000-row OrderDetail table unexpectedly returns 50 million rows instead of something in the few-hundred-thousand range. What almost certainly went wrong, and how would you confirm it?
questions.modelAnswer: 50 million is exactly 500 times 100,000 -- the row-count signature of a Cartesian product, where every row of one table gets paired with every row of the other instead of only matching rows being paired. The most common real-world cause isn't a deliberate CROSS JOIN -- it's a missing or ineffective ON condition on what was meant to be a normal join: either the ON clause is left out entirely (old-style comma join with no join condition), or it exists but evaluates to true for nearly every row combination (for example ON p.Name IS NOT NULL, which doesn't actually relate the two tables). To confirm it, check the join's ON clause first for a missing or non-relating condition, and as a general habit, sanity-check the row count after any join: if two tables of roughly 500 and 100,000 rows produce millions of result rows instead of a number in that rough range, that's an immediate signal to re-check the ON clause rather than assume the data is simply that large.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd notice is that 50 million is suspiciously close to 500 times 100,000 -- that's the fingerprint of a Cartesian product, not a coincidence. My first move is to go straight to the ON clause of the join and check two things: is it missing entirely, which happens with old comma-style joins that have no join condition at all, or does it exist but not actually relate the two tables -- something like ON p.Name IS NOT NULL, which is true for almost every row and produces a Cartesian product in disguise even though there's technically an ON clause sitting there. Once I fix the condition to something that actually ties the tables together, like p.ProductID = sod.ProductID, I'd re-run the query and expect the row count to land in the same rough range as the bigger of the two tables, not multiply them together. I've made this a habit on every join I write now: sanity-check the row count before trusting the result.
questions.example:
-- BUG: no join condition at all -- a Cartesian product
SELECT p.Name, sod.OrderQty
FROM Production.Product AS p, Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod;

-- BUG: ON clause exists but doesn't relate the tables
SELECT p.Name, sod.OrderQty
FROM Production.Product AS p
INNER JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod
    ON p.Name IS NOT NULL;

-- FIXED: a real join condition tying the tables together
SELECT p.Name, sod.OrderQty
FROM Production.Product AS p
INNER JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod
    ON p.ProductID = sod.ProductID;
commonMistakes: Assuming the data itself is just 'that big' instead of suspecting the join condition first
Not recognizing that an ON clause can exist and still produce a Cartesian product if it doesn't genuinely relate the tables
Never sanity-checking row counts after writing a join, so the problem isn't caught until it hits production
Confusing this with a deliberate CROSS JOIN -- the accidental version almost always comes from a broken or missing ON condition on what was meant to be a normal join
keyPoints: Row count multiplying (500 x 100,000) instead of adding is the signature of a Cartesian product
Most accidental Cartesian products come from a missing or non-relating ON clause
Old-style comma joins with no ON clause default to a Cartesian product
An ON clause that's technically present but true for nearly every row is just as dangerous as none at all
Sanity-check row counts after any join as a standing habit

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the Cartesian product and the row-count math
Correctly identifies missing/ineffective ON clause as the cause
Describes a practical way to catch this before production

questions.title: Inflated totals after a new relationship
questions.prompt: A Power BI report's total sales figure looks inflated after a new relationship was added between two tables, and that relationship's cardinality was automatically set to 'one to one.' What might be wrong, and how would incorrect cardinality cause this?
questions.modelAnswer: Power BI sets cardinality to one-to-one automatically when it notices a value never repeats on either side of the relationship at the time the relationship is created. If the underlying data later changes so that one side starts legitimately repeating values (for example, a second budget row gets added for the same project in a later refresh), that one-to-one relationship no longer reflects reality, and Power BI's query engine will treat each row match as unique when it isn't -- a many-side table with duplicated keys joined as if it were one-to-one can fan out matching rows and inflate a SUM measure, because the engine isn't aggregating correctly across what are actually multiple matching rows per key. The fix is to open Manage relationships, edit the relationship, and override the cardinality to 'many to one' (or 'one to many'), explicitly pointing the 'many' side at the table that actually repeats values, rather than trusting Power BI's automatic detection once the data's shape has changed.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move would be Manage relationships, to actually see what cardinality Power BI chose and why. One-to-one only gets picked automatically because, at the moment the relationship was created, Power BI genuinely didn't see any repeated values on either side -- but that's a snapshot of the data at one point in time, not a guarantee. If a later refresh adds a second row for the same key on one side -- say a second budget line for a project that used to have exactly one -- the relationship is now lying about the data's actual shape, and a SUM measure built on top of it can double-count or otherwise misbehave because the engine is still treating the join as strictly one-to-one. The fix is straightforward once I've diagnosed it: edit the relationship and explicitly set cardinality to many-to-one, with the 'many' side pointed at whichever table I know will eventually repeat values, rather than leaving it to Power BI's automatic guess.
commonMistakes: Trusting Power BI's automatically-detected cardinality permanently instead of re-checking it after the data's shape changes
Not realizing one-to-one is only ever a snapshot judgment based on the data present when the relationship was created
Looking everywhere except Manage relationships when a total looks wrong after a schema change
Not knowing which side of a mismatched relationship should be set to 'many'
keyPoints: Power BI auto-detects one-to-one only when no repeats exist on either side at creation time
If repeats appear later, a stale one-to-one relationship can cause incorrect aggregation
Check and, if needed, manually override cardinality in Manage relationships
Point the 'many' side at whichever table is known to eventually repeat values

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses stale/incorrect cardinality as the likely cause
Explains how that causes inflated aggregation
Proposes the correct fix (Manage relationships, override cardinality)

questions.title: A slicer that silently doesn't filter
questions.prompt: A Power BI model has two relationships between the Sales table and the Date table -- one on OrderDate and one on ShipDate. A slicer built on the Date table filters visuals using OrderDate correctly, but a separate visual that's supposed to use ShipDate doesn't react to the slicer at all. What's almost certainly going on, and how would you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: Power BI only allows one active relationship between any two given tables at a time, so that every filter path through the model stays unambiguous. With two relationships between Sales and Date (OrderDate and ShipDate), only one can be active (shown as a solid line); the other is automatically made inactive (a dashed line in the model view) and does not propagate filters on its own at all -- a slicer built on Date simply has no effect on anything meant to rely on the inactive relationship. Editing the relationship to make ShipDate active wouldn't fix this -- it would just flip which relationship is inactive, since the one-active-at-a-time rule doesn't go away. The real fix is a measure that explicitly activates the inactive relationship for just that calculation: CALCULATE(<expression>, USERELATIONSHIP(Sales[ShipDate], 'Date'[Date])). Any visual that needs to filter by ShipDate has to use a measure built with USERELATIONSHIP; a plain SUM(Sales[Amount]) dropped into a visual keeps using whichever relationship is active, regardless of which date field happens to be on that visual's axis.
questions.professionalAnswer: The dashed line in the model view is the first thing I'd check, because that's Power BI's visual signal for an inactive relationship. Two relationships between the same pair of tables means only one gets to be active -- that's not a bug, it's by design, so there's always exactly one unambiguous filter path between any two tables. Flipping which one is active in Manage Relationships doesn't actually solve this; it just swaps which one is now inactive. What I'd do instead is write a measure specifically for the ShipDate-based visual using CALCULATE with USERELATIONSHIP(Sales[ShipDate], 'Date'[Date]) wrapped around it, which activates that relationship for just this one calculation. A plain SUM measure on that same visual would still silently follow the active OrderDate relationship no matter what's on the axis, which is exactly the confusing symptom described here.
questions.example:
-- Ship Date Sales = CALCULATE(
--     SUM(Sales[Amount]),
--     USERELATIONSHIP(Sales[ShipDate], 'Date'[Date])
-- )
-- Activates the normally-inactive ShipDate relationship for just this measure.
commonMistakes: Trying to make the ShipDate relationship active in Manage Relationships, not realizing that just makes OrderDate inactive instead -- only one can be active at a time
Not noticing the dashed line in the model diagram, which is Power BI's visual signal for an inactive relationship
Assuming a visual will automatically use the 'other' relationship just because that date field is on the visual's axis
Forgetting USERELATIONSHIP only works inside CALCULATE, and only activates the relationship for that one measure's evaluation
keyPoints: Power BI allows only one active relationship between any two tables at a time
The second relationship becomes inactive automatically, shown as a dashed line
An inactive relationship does not propagate filters until explicitly activated
USERELATIONSHIP inside CALCULATE activates an inactive relationship for one measure's calculation

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the inactive-relationship cause
Correctly explains why only one relationship can be active
Proposes the correct fix (USERELATIONSHIP inside CALCULATE)

questions.title: SUM inflated after joining a one-to-many table
questions.prompt: A query joins SalesOrderHeader to SalesOrderDetail and correctly totals each order with SUM(LineTotal). After adding a third join to a Promotion table -- where some orders have more than one matching promotion row -- the total for those specific orders suddenly doubles or triples, even though nothing about the actual sales changed. The join conditions are all correct and genuinely relate the tables. What's going on, and how would you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: This isn't a Cartesian product -- every join condition is correct and genuinely relates the tables -- it's join fan-out, which happens whenever a correct join still has a one-to-many relationship on one side. Each SalesOrderDetail row that matches more than one Promotion row gets physically duplicated once per matching promotion before SUM ever runs, so SUM(LineTotal) is now adding the same line total two or three times for any order whose promotion happens to match more than once, while orders with exactly one (or zero) matching promotions are unaffected. The fix is to never combine two separate one-to-many expansions in a single flat join and then aggregate at the end -- instead, pre-aggregate each one-to-many relationship to the grain actually needed, in its own subquery or CTE, before joining. Here, that means computing the order total from SalesOrderHeader and SalesOrderDetail alone first, and only joining Promotion afterward (or in a separate query) if promotion details are genuinely needed, rather than letting its fan-out multiply rows that feed directly into the order-total SUM.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd point out first that this isn't the Cartesian-product bug people usually learn about -- every join condition here is correct and really does relate the tables. This is fan-out: joining in a table that can legitimately match more than one row per order duplicates the order-detail rows underneath it, once per matching promotion, before the SUM even runs. So an order with two matching promotions gets its LineTotal counted twice, not because the math is wrong, but because the row genuinely got duplicated first. My fix is to separate the two aggregations: compute each order's total from just SalesOrderHeader and SalesOrderDetail in a CTE first, completely isolated from the Promotion join, and only bring Promotion into a separate query (or join it after the order total is already locked in) if I actually need promotion-level detail. The rule I'd apply going forward is never to let two independent one-to-many joins sit in the same flat query feeding one aggregate -- pre-aggregate each one to the grain I need first.
questions.example:
-- WRONG: Promotion's fan-out inflates the order total
SELECT soh.SalesOrderID, SUM(sod.LineTotal) AS OrderTotal
FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader soh
JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail sod ON sod.SalesOrderID = soh.SalesOrderID
JOIN Sales.SpecialOfferProduct promo ON promo.ProductID = sod.ProductID
GROUP BY soh.SalesOrderID;

-- FIXED: order total computed in isolation, before any promotion join
WITH OrderTotals AS (
    SELECT soh.SalesOrderID, SUM(sod.LineTotal) AS OrderTotal
    FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader soh
    JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail sod ON sod.SalesOrderID = soh.SalesOrderID
    GROUP BY soh.SalesOrderID
)
SELECT * FROM OrderTotals;
commonMistakes: Assuming a correct, relating join condition rules out row duplication entirely
Not comparing row counts (or a known-good total) before and after adding the third join
Reaching for SUM(DISTINCT ...) as a quick fix, which only coincidentally works and breaks again as soon as two genuinely different line totals happen to match
Combining two separate one-to-many expansions in one flat query feeding a single aggregate, instead of pre-aggregating each one to the grain actually needed
keyPoints: A correct join condition can still fan out rows when the relationship is genuinely one-to-many
Fan-out duplicates rows before aggregation runs, inflating any SUM downstream
This is distinct from a Cartesian product, which comes from a missing or non-relating join condition
Fix: pre-aggregate each one-to-many relationship to the needed grain in its own subquery/CTE before joining further

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses join fan-out (not a Cartesian product)
Explains why the duplication inflates the SUM
Proposes a correct fix (pre-aggregating before joining further)

questions.title: COPY INTO says 0 rows loaded after fixing a file
questions.prompt: You run COPY INTO to load a file from a stage, and it fails partway through with a data error. You fix the bad rows in the source file, re-upload it to the same stage under the same file name, and re-run the exact same COPY INTO statement -- but it reports 0 rows loaded, as if nothing happened. What's going on, and how do you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: Snowflake tracks the load history of every file loaded into a table through COPY INTO, keyed by file name and a checksum of its contents, for 64 days by default -- this is what normally prevents the same file from being accidentally loaded twice. If the file that originally failed still got partially recorded as 'loaded' (or if a file with the same name was already loaded successfully once before, even under different circumstances), Snowflake sees a file with that name already in its load history and skips it entirely on the next COPY INTO, reporting 0 rows loaded rather than an error -- which is correct, deliberate dedup behavior, not a bug, but it's confusing the first time you hit it. The fix is to force Snowflake to reload the file despite its load history, using COPY INTO ... FORCE = TRUE, which bypasses the file-level dedup check for this one load. A more targeted alternative, if only one file is affected, is removing that specific file's entry from the load history (or renaming the corrected file before re-uploading it) so Snowflake treats it as new.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd check is Snowflake's load history for that table, because '0 rows loaded with no error' is almost always Snowflake telling me, correctly, that it already thinks it loaded this exact file. Snowflake tracks loaded files by name and a checksum for 64 days specifically to stop the same file from being double-loaded by accident, and re-uploading a corrected file under the identical name doesn't automatically reset that. The fix is adding FORCE = TRUE to the COPY INTO statement, which tells Snowflake to ignore that history and reload the file regardless. I'd use that deliberately and sparingly, though, since FORCE = TRUE is also exactly how you'd accidentally double-load a file that genuinely was already loaded correctly -- so I only reach for it once I've actually confirmed, via the load history, that this specific file is the one that needs a forced reload.
commonMistakes: Assuming 0 rows loaded with no error means the file is empty or malformed, instead of checking load history first
Not knowing Snowflake tracks loaded files by name and checksum for 64 days by default
Using FORCE = TRUE as a default habit on every load instead of only after confirming via load history that it's actually needed
Renaming the file as a workaround without understanding why it works (a new name has no prior load history entry)
keyPoints: Snowflake tracks loaded files by file name and checksum, for 64 days by default, to prevent duplicate loads
0 rows loaded with no error usually means the file already appears in that load history
COPY INTO ... FORCE = TRUE bypasses the load-history check and reloads the file regardless
Check load history before using FORCE, to avoid accidentally double-loading a file that was already loaded correctly

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the load-history/dedup behavior as the cause
Correctly proposes FORCE = TRUE as the fix
Notes the risk of using FORCE carelessly

questions.title: A dbt not_null test starts failing after a source change
questions.prompt: A not_null test on customer_id in your stg_customers model has passed for months. After a change to the upstream source system, dbt test suddenly reports 12 failures on that same test. What are the two fundamentally different explanations for this, and how do you tell which one you're dealing with?
questions.modelAnswer: The first explanation is a genuine data quality problem: the upstream source system actually started producing rows with a missing customer_id, and the test is doing exactly its job by catching that before it reaches a downstream mart or report. The second explanation is that the staging model's logic itself broke -- for example, a join or a rename introduced earlier in the model now produces a NULL in a column that previously never would have been NULL, meaning the test is correctly flagging a bug that's actually in the transformation, not in the source. The way to tell which one it is: query the raw source table directly (bypassing the staging model entirely) and check whether those same specific rows already have a NULL or missing customer_id at the source. If the raw data already has the NULL, it's a genuine upstream data quality issue to raise with whoever owns that source system. If the raw data has a valid customer_id for those rows but the staging model's own output doesn't, the bug is in the model's transformation logic, not the source data -- most commonly a join that's dropping or nulling a value that existed correctly beforehand.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't assume either direction automatically -- a sudden failure on a test that's passed for months could mean the source genuinely started sending bad data, or it could mean something in my own model broke. My first move is going straight to the raw source table and checking those exact 12 rows directly, with none of my staging model's logic involved at all. If the source itself already shows a NULL customer_id on those rows, that's a real upstream data quality issue, and the test did exactly its job -- I'd flag it to whoever owns that source system rather than trying to patch around it in my model. If the source has a perfectly valid customer_id for those rows but my staging model's output doesn't, the bug is mine, most likely a join or a case statement I added that's quietly nulling out a value that used to come through fine. Either way, the test failing is a good outcome -- it caught something before a downstream report did.
commonMistakes: Assuming a test failure after a source change must be a real data quality problem, without checking whether the model's own logic is actually the cause
Assuming a test failure must be a bug in the model, without checking whether the source data genuinely changed
Patching the model to silently coalesce the NULL to a default value instead of determining the actual root cause first
Not isolating the check by querying the raw source table directly, separate from the staging model's transformation
keyPoints: A test failure can mean a genuine upstream data quality problem, or a bug introduced in the model's own transformation logic
Query the raw source table directly, bypassing the model, to see which side the NULL actually originates from
A genuine source problem should be raised with whoever owns the source system, not silently patched
A test catching a real problem -- either kind -- is the test working correctly, not a nuisance to suppress

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies both possible explanations
Describes a correct method for distinguishing them (checking raw source directly)
Avoids jumping to silently patching without diagnosing first

questions.title: dbt run fails with 'relation does not exist'
questions.prompt: Running dbt run produces 'Database Error: relation RAW.CUSTOMERS does not exist' for a model that uses source('raw', 'customers'), even though you can see the CUSTOMERS table sitting right there in Snowflake. What's the most likely cause, and how would you check it?
questions.modelAnswer: source() doesn't look at the table name alone -- it resolves to the database and schema defined for that source in sources.yml, combined with the table name given in the source() call. The most likely cause is a mismatch between what sources.yml declares (the database and schema it says 'raw' points to) and where the table actually lives in Snowflake -- for example, sources.yml pointing at a database/schema the current dbt target doesn't have access to, or the table genuinely existing in a different schema than sources.yml claims. It can also happen if the dbt profile being used for this run points at the wrong Snowflake database/role entirely, so the connection itself is looking in the wrong place. To check, open sources.yml and confirm the exact database and schema configured there, then run a plain SELECT against that exact fully-qualified name directly in a Snowflake worksheet (not through dbt) using the same role the dbt connection uses -- if that direct query also fails, the issue is a genuine location or permissions mismatch, not a dbt-specific bug.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd check isn't the table itself, it's sources.yml, because source() doesn't magically find a table by name -- it resolves to whatever database and schema that source is configured to point at. If sources.yml says the 'raw' source lives in a different database or schema than where CUSTOMERS actually sits, dbt will generate a reference to a location that genuinely doesn't exist, even though the table is sitting right there somewhere else. I'd also check which Snowflake role and database the dbt connection is actually using for this run -- a profile pointed at the wrong role can fail to see a table that's visible to me personally in the Snowflake UI, purely because of permissions. My actual check is running the exact fully-qualified name dbt is generating as a plain SELECT directly in Snowflake, using that same role -- if that fails too, it confirms this isn't a dbt problem at all, it's a location or permissions mismatch.

Not checking which role/database the dbt connection profile is actually using for this run
Editing the model's SQL directly instead of fixing the actual source configuration in sources.yml
Not testing the exact fully-qualified name dbt generates directly in Snowflake to isolate whether it's a dbt problem or a Snowflake access problem
keyPoints: source() resolves to the database/schema configured in sources.yml, not just the table name given
A mismatch between sources.yml's configured location and the table's actual location causes this error
The dbt connection's role/database can also cause this if it lacks visibility into the table's actual location
Test the exact fully-qualified name directly in Snowflake, with the same role, to isolate dbt from the underlying access issue

Mentions the dbt connection's role/database as a related possible cause

questions.title: A new DAG isn't showing up in the Airflow UI at all
questions.prompt: You save a new DAG file into the dags folder, but after waiting several minutes, it never appears in the Airflow UI at all -- not even as a broken DAG. Where do you look, and what's the most likely cause?
questions.modelAnswer: The Airflow scheduler periodically scans the dags folder and tries to parse (import) every Python file it finds there -- 'tries to parse,' not 'successfully loads,' is the key distinction. If a DAG file has a Python syntax error or raises an exception at import time (a typo, a missing import, an indentation error), the scheduler fails to parse that file entirely and it never becomes a DAG object the UI can display -- which is why it doesn't even show up as a broken/red DAG, it simply doesn't exist from the UI's point of view. The place to look is the Airflow UI's own 'DAG Import Errors' panel (usually shown at the top of the DAGs list, or under Browse), which surfaces the exact Python exception and traceback for any file the scheduler couldn't import -- that's almost always faster and more direct than digging through raw scheduler logs. The fix is reading that traceback and correcting the actual Python error in the file; once it imports cleanly, the DAG appears in the UI on the next scheduler scan.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first stop is the DAG Import Errors panel right in the Airflow UI, not the scheduler logs, because that's specifically built to surface exactly this situation -- a file in the dags folder that the scheduler tried to import and couldn't. A DAG that never appears at all, not even broken, almost always means a Python-level problem in the file itself: a typo, a bad import, an indentation mistake -- something that throws an exception before Airflow ever gets to the point of registering it as a DAG object. The import errors panel shows me the actual traceback, which is usually enough to point straight at the broken line. Once I fix that specific error and save the file again, I just wait for the next scheduler scan and it shows up normally -- there's no restart or redeploy needed for a simple syntax fix like that in most setups.

Digging through full scheduler logs before checking the dedicated DAG Import Errors panel, which surfaces this directly
Not realizing a DAG with an import-time exception won't appear even as a 'broken' DAG -- it simply won't exist in the UI at all
Assuming a fix requires restarting the scheduler, when the next automatic folder scan picks up a corrected file
keyPoints: The scheduler periodically scans and tries to import every file in the dags folder
A Python exception at import time means the DAG never gets registered -- it won't appear even as broken
The DAG Import Errors panel in the UI shows the exact traceback for any file that failed to import
Fixing the Python error and waiting for the next scan is usually all that's needed, no restart required

Correctly names the DAG Import Errors panel as where to look
Describes the correct resolution path

questions.title: A task is stuck in 'queued' and never starts running
questions.prompt: A DAG is scheduled correctly and shows up fine in the Airflow UI, but when it triggers, its tasks sit in a 'queued' state indefinitely and never move to 'running.' What are the most likely causes, and what would you check first?
questions.modelAnswer: 'Queued' means Airflow has decided a task is ready to run and has handed it off to be executed, but no actual worker process has picked it up yet -- the DAG and scheduling logic are working correctly; the problem is downstream, in execution capacity. The most common cause is that the executor (Celery, Kubernetes, or similar, depending on the setup) simply doesn't have any available worker to run the task -- either no worker process is running at all, or every available worker slot is already occupied by other tasks. A second common cause is a pool or concurrency limit -- Airflow lets you cap how many tasks can run simultaneously (globally, per-DAG, or via a named pool), and a task stuck in queued can simply be waiting for a slot that's fully occupied by other tasks. The first checks: confirm the worker process is actually running and reachable (not crashed or never started), and check whether a concurrency or pool limit is currently maxed out by other running tasks.
questions.professionalAnswer: 'Queued' tells me something specific: Airflow's scheduler has already decided this task is ready to go, so the DAG logic and scheduling aren't the problem here -- the problem is that nothing has actually picked the task up to run it yet. My first check is whether a worker is even running -- if the worker process crashed or was never started, tasks will queue forever with nothing wrong on the DAG side at all. If a worker is running, my next check is concurrency limits -- Airflow lets you cap how many tasks run at once, globally or through a named pool, and if every slot is already taken by other tasks, a newly queued task just waits its turn. I'd check both of those before assuming anything is actually wrong with the DAG itself, since a correctly-defined DAG stuck in queued is almost always an infrastructure/capacity issue, not a DAG-authoring one.

Not checking whether the worker process is actually running at all
Forgetting that concurrency or pool limits can hold a correctly-scheduled task in queued indefinitely
Restarting or rewriting the DAG before checking whether the issue is actually infrastructure-level

Check first whether a worker process is actually running and reachable
Check concurrency/pool limits, which can hold a valid task in queued if all slots are occupied
A correctly-defined DAG stuck in queued usually points to infrastructure/capacity, not DAG authoring

questions.title: Power BI Desktop vs. the Power BI Service
questions.prompt: What's the architectural difference between Power BI Desktop and the Power BI Service, and why does a report usually need both instead of just one or the other?
questions.modelAnswer: Power BI Desktop is a free, locally-installed Windows application where all of the authoring happens -- connecting to data sources, building the data model and DAX measures in Power Query and the model view, and designing the actual report visuals. It produces a single .pbix file that lives on the author's own machine until it's deliberately published. The Power BI Service (app.powerbi.com) is the cloud-hosted side -- a published report lives inside a workspace there, where it can be shared with other people, scheduled for automatic data refresh, organized into an App for wider distribution, and secured with row-level security role assignments. The split exists because authoring (building a model, writing measures, designing visuals) and consumption/distribution (viewing, sharing, scheduling, securing) are genuinely different jobs with different audiences: one author builds in Desktop, then publishes once to the Service so many viewers can consume it without ever touching Desktop or the underlying model. Some things can only happen in the Service (scheduled refresh against on-premises data via a gateway, app distribution, RLS role assignment) and some only in Desktop (building or materially changing the data model) -- which is exactly why most real projects move back and forth between the two rather than picking only one.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe Desktop as the workshop and the Service as the storefront. Desktop is where I actually build things -- the model, the measures, the report layout -- all saved into one .pbix file that nobody else can see until I choose to publish it. The Service is where that finished work actually reaches people: it lives in a workspace, it can be shared, it can be scheduled to refresh on its own overnight, and it's the only place I can assign a specific person to a row-level-security role. I couldn't do RLS assignment or scheduled refresh from inside Desktop even if I wanted to -- those are Service-only capabilities -- and I can't materially change the data model from inside the Service, so a real change still has to start back in Desktop and get republished. That back-and-forth isn't a workaround, it's just how the two pieces are meant to work together.
commonMistakes: Thinking the Power BI Service is just a web version of Desktop instead of a separate hosting/distribution layer
Trying to assign RLS role membership inside Desktop, which isn't possible there
Forgetting a report has to be deliberately published from Desktop before it exists in the Service at all
Not realizing scheduled, unattended data refresh is a Service feature, not something Desktop does on its own
keyPoints: Power BI Desktop: local authoring tool, produces a .pbix file, where the model and visuals are built
Power BI Service: cloud hosting/distribution layer -- sharing, scheduled refresh, apps, RLS assignment
Authoring and distribution are different jobs with different audiences
Some features exist only in Desktop (model building) and some only in the Service (RLS assignment, scheduled refresh, apps)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes Desktop's authoring role from the Service's hosting/distribution role

questions.title: Why Dev, QA, and Production stay separate
questions.prompt: Why does a BI team typically maintain separate Dev, QA, and Production SQL Server environments, and promote a change through them in that fixed order, instead of just building and testing directly against the Production database that live reports and real users already depend on?
questions.modelAnswer: Dev is where new work is actually built, and it's expected to be unstable -- half-finished packages, broken queries, and throwaway test data are all normal there, and critically, none of that instability is visible to anyone who depends on real numbers. QA is a separate, more stable environment with data that resembles Production, used specifically to verify a change behaves correctly before any real user is ever exposed to it -- this is where testing is supposed to happen, not in Dev and not in Production. Production is the environment real business users and live reports actually run against, and it's deliberately the last environment any change reaches, only after being built in Dev and then validated in QA. Testing directly against Production is risky for two concrete reasons: an in-progress or buggy change can lock, corrupt, or simply show wrong numbers in data that live reports depend on right now, and there's no safe way to test something genuinely risky -- a schema change, a large bulk load -- without potentially causing a real outage if it goes wrong. Promoting a change through Dev, then QA, then Production in that fixed order guarantees every change gets at least one chance to fail somewhere that doesn't matter yet before it ever reaches somewhere that does.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame it around what's allowed to break where. Dev is allowed to break -- that's the whole point of it, it's where I'm actively building and nobody real is looking at it. QA is where I prove a change actually works against data that looks like the real thing, before any real user sees it. Production is the one environment where breaking something has an actual business cost, so it's deliberately the last stop, not the first. If I skipped straight to testing in Production, the two real risks are: a change that's still buggy could corrupt or lock data that a live report is reading from right now, and there's no safe way to rehearse something genuinely risky, like a schema change, without actually risking the outage I was trying to avoid. The fixed Dev-then-QA-then-Production order is really just making sure every change gets tested somewhere low-stakes before it reaches somewhere high-stakes.
commonMistakes: Making a direct change in Production 'just this once' to save time
Treating QA as optional for a change that 'seems small' instead of validating it there first
Letting QA's data drift so far from Production's that it stops catching real issues
Conflating Dev and QA as the same environment instead of recognizing their different purposes (building vs. validating)
keyPoints: Dev is for building and is expected to be unstable, isolated from real users
QA validates a change against production-like data before any real user is exposed to it
Production is the last environment reached, only after Dev and QA
Direct Production changes risk live data and can't safely rehearse risky operations

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the purpose of each environment (Dev, QA, Production)
Correctly explains the risk of testing directly in Production
Explains why the promotion order matters

questions.title: Why the semantic model is its own layer
questions.prompt: In Power BI, what is a semantic model (also called a dataset), and why is it treated as a layer separate from any one report built on top of it? What becomes possible once you realize several different reports can all point at the very same semantic model?
questions.modelAnswer: A semantic model is the published data model itself -- tables, relationships, calculated columns, measures, and RLS roles -- without any particular report's visuals attached to it; it's the single source of truth layer sitting between raw data and however many reports choose to visualize it. Publishing a single .pbix that has both a model and report visuals does create a semantic model and a report together by default, but once published, the semantic model exists in the workspace as its own independent object. Any report author with the right permission can then build a brand-new report connected to that existing semantic model (through Create report, or a Live Connection) without rebuilding the tables, relationships, or measures from scratch. This matters because it means business logic -- how a measure is calculated, which relationships are correct, who can see which rows under RLS -- is defined exactly once, and every report built against that semantic model automatically inherits the same correct logic; if a measure's definition ever needs fixing, fixing it once in the semantic model updates every report built on top of it, instead of requiring the same fix to be found and repeated across several separately-built reports.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe the semantic model as the thing that actually has the business logic in it -- the relationships, the measures, the RLS roles -- completely separate from however a given report chooses to visualize that logic. Publishing one .pbix does hand you both a semantic model and a report at the same time, but they're two separate objects the moment they land in the workspace, and that's exactly what lets a finance team build one report and an executive-summary team build a completely different-looking report, both connected live to that same underlying semantic model, without either of them re-deriving what 'Total Revenue' actually means. The real payoff is maintenance: if I find a bug in a measure, I fix it once, in the semantic model, and every report built on top of it -- including ones I didn't build myself -- picks up the fix automatically, instead of me having to track down and patch the same formula in five separate files.
commonMistakes: Rebuilding the same measures and relationships from scratch in every new report instead of connecting to the existing semantic model
Thinking a published semantic model and a published report are the same object
Not realizing RLS lives on the semantic model, so it applies consistently to every report connected to it
Forgetting a Live Connection report depends on that semantic model staying published and accessible
keyPoints: A semantic model is the data model (tables, relationships, measures, RLS) without any one report's visuals
Publishing a .pbix creates a semantic model and a report, but they become separate objects in the workspace
Multiple reports can connect to one shared semantic model via Live Connection
Fixing logic once in the semantic model updates every report built on top of it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines a semantic model and what it contains
Correctly explains that it's a separate object from any one report
Explains the maintenance/consistency benefit of multiple reports sharing one model

questions.title: Why use dbt instead of a folder of SQL scripts
questions.prompt: A team currently transforms data by running a folder of hand-written SQL scripts in a particular order, with a README explaining which script depends on which. Why would you recommend moving that to dbt instead, even though dbt models are still, underneath, just SQL SELECT statements?
questions.modelAnswer: A folder of scripts with a README describing run order has no way to actually enforce that order -- if someone runs script 3 before script 2 by mistake, nothing stops them, and nothing catches it until something downstream breaks or shows wrong data. dbt's ref() function replaces that README with something dbt itself can read and enforce: every ref() call becomes an edge in a dependency graph, and dbt automatically computes and runs models in the correct order every single time, with no human having to remember or follow written instructions. A folder of scripts also has no equivalent to dbt's built-in testing (not_null, unique, relationships, custom tests) running automatically after each build, no auto-generated documentation describing what each transformation does and how tables relate, and no single command that rebuilds only what actually changed. The underlying SQL complexity is genuinely the same either way -- dbt doesn't make the transformations themselves simpler -- but it wraps that SQL in dependency management, testing, and documentation that a plain folder of scripts has no structural way to provide.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd point out that the actual SQL doesn't get any smarter just by moving it into dbt -- a SELECT statement is a SELECT statement either way. What changes is everything around it. A README saying 'run script 2 before script 3' is a suggestion a person has to remember and follow correctly every time; ref() is dbt actually enforcing that order itself, every single run, with zero chance of a human running things out of sequence. On top of that, I get testing almost for free -- not_null and unique checks that run automatically after a model builds, which a folder of scripts has no structural equivalent for at all. And I get documentation and a dependency graph generated directly from the project itself, instead of a README that's one undocumented change away from being wrong. None of that makes the transformation logic itself less complex -- it just stops relying on a human correctly following written instructions to get that logic to run in the right order with any kind of safety net.
commonMistakes: Assuming dbt makes the SQL itself simpler, rather than adding dependency management, testing, and documentation around the same SQL
Not recognizing that a README-documented run order has no enforcement mechanism at all
Overlooking dbt's built-in testing as a structural advantage a folder of scripts has no equivalent for
Treating this as purely a tooling preference instead of a real reliability/maintainability difference
keyPoints: A folder of scripts relies on a human correctly following a README's stated run order, with nothing enforcing it
dbt's ref() function builds an actual dependency graph that's automatically and correctly ordered every run
dbt adds built-in testing and auto-generated documentation that a script folder has no structural equivalent for
The SQL's own complexity is unchanged -- dbt adds structure and safety around it, not simpler SQL

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the dependency-enforcement advantage (ref() vs. a README)
Correctly identifies testing/documentation as additional structural advantages
Correctly notes the underlying SQL complexity is unchanged

questions.title: Why split dbt models into staging, intermediate, and marts layers
questions.prompt: Why do dbt projects conventionally split models into three layers -- staging, intermediate, and marts -- instead of writing one larger model that goes straight from raw source data to a finished, business-ready table?
questions.modelAnswer: Each layer has a distinct, narrow job, which is what makes the overall project maintainable as it grows. Staging models do a thin, one-to-one cleanup of exactly one raw source -- renaming columns, fixing types -- and nothing more structural. Intermediate models combine or reshape more than one staging model to build a reusable, meaningful concept (joining orders to customers, for example) that isn't yet final reporting output. Marts models are the final, business-ready tables that reporting tools actually query, often further combining intermediate models into the shape a dashboard or report needs. Writing one large model that jumps straight from raw to final output collapses all three jobs into one -- which means a single model becomes the only place a rename, a join bug, and final business logic can all hide at once, making it far harder to isolate where a problem actually is. The layered approach also means the same intermediate concept -- a 'customer orders' building block, say -- can be reused by multiple different marts without being rebuilt or recomputed separately in each one, since it already exists as its own model that other models can just ref().
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame it as separation of concerns, the same reason you wouldn't want one giant function doing input validation, business logic, and formatting output all in the same fifty lines. Staging's only job is a clean rename of exactly one raw source -- nothing structural. Intermediate takes a couple of staging models and builds a real, reusable concept out of them. Marts is the final, business-ready table reporting tools actually query. If I collapse all of that into one big model, and something's wrong with the output, I have no way to isolate whether it's a renaming mistake, a join bug, or the final business logic -- it's all tangled together in one place. Splitting it up also means if two different marts both need the same 'customer orders' concept, I build that once as an intermediate model and ref() it from both, instead of recomputing the same join twice in two separate giant models.
commonMistakes: Collapsing staging, intermediate, and business logic into one model, making it hard to isolate where a bug actually is
Not recognizing that an intermediate model can be reused by multiple downstream marts instead of rebuilt per mart
Treating the layering as arbitrary convention rather than a real separation-of-concerns benefit
Putting business/reporting logic into a staging model instead of keeping staging strictly thin
keyPoints: Staging: thin, one-to-one cleanup of exactly one raw source
Intermediate: combines staging models into a reusable, meaningful concept, not yet final output
Marts: final, business-ready tables that reporting tools actually query
Layering isolates where a bug lives and lets intermediate concepts be reused across multiple marts

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the distinct job of each of the three layers
Explains the maintainability/debuggability benefit of separating them
Explains the reuse benefit of an intermediate layer

questions.title: Why orchestrate with Airflow instead of a cron job or Task Scheduler
questions.prompt: A pipeline currently runs as a Windows Task Scheduler job that kicks off a script once a night. Why would you recommend moving that to Airflow once the pipeline grows to several dependent steps, instead of just adding more scheduled scripts?
questions.modelAnswer: A scheduler like Task Scheduler or cron is good at exactly one thing: triggering a script at a fixed time. It has no concept of a dependency between two separate scheduled jobs -- if job B needs job A to finish first, the only way to enforce that with plain scheduling is guessing a safe time gap between them and hoping job A always finishes within that window, which becomes fragile and eventually wrong as job A's runtime varies. It also has no built-in retry logic for a single failed step, no visibility into which specific step failed versus which succeeded, and no easy way to re-run just the one step that failed without re-running everything. Airflow's DAG model replaces guessed time gaps with explicit dependencies (A must actually complete before B starts, regardless of how long A took), gives each task its own retry policy, and provides a UI showing exactly which task succeeded, failed, or is still running, plus the ability to re-run just one failed task without re-triggering the whole pipeline. The point where this switch becomes worth it is specifically when a pipeline grows multiple genuinely dependent steps -- a single standalone nightly script has little reason to move to Airflow at all; the value appears once ordering, retries, and partial-failure visibility actually start to matter.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd say the core issue with chaining Task Scheduler jobs is that there's no real dependency between them -- just a guessed time gap. If job A usually takes 20 minutes, I'd schedule job B to start 30 minutes later and hope that's always enough of a buffer, but the day job A runs long, job B starts against incomplete data with nothing catching that. Airflow replaces that guess with an actual dependency: B simply doesn't start until A has genuinely finished successfully, no matter how long A took. I'd also point out the visibility difference -- when something fails at 2 AM, Task Scheduler gives me very little to go on, while Airflow's UI shows me exactly which task in the chain failed, lets me retry just that one task, and can alert me automatically. I wouldn't necessarily move a single standalone script to Airflow just because it's nightly -- the real trigger for making this move is once there are genuinely multiple dependent steps where getting the order and retries right actually starts to matter.
commonMistakes: Scheduling dependent jobs with guessed time gaps instead of enforcing a real completion-based dependency
Not recognizing the retry and partial-failure-visibility gap in a plain scheduler compared to Airflow
Recommending Airflow for a single standalone script that has no actual dependencies to manage
Assuming the migration is purely about scheduling syntax rather than dependency enforcement and observability
keyPoints: A plain scheduler (cron/Task Scheduler) has no concept of a dependency between separate jobs, only guessed time gaps
Airflow enforces real completion-based dependencies between tasks, regardless of how long any one task takes
Airflow provides retry logic, per-task status visibility, and the ability to re-run just one failed task
The move is worth it once a pipeline has multiple genuinely dependent steps, not for a single standalone script

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the dependency-enforcement gap in a plain scheduler
Correctly identifies the retry/visibility advantages of Airflow
Correctly scopes when this move is actually worth making

questions.title: How Snowflake, dbt, and Airflow fit together end to end
questions.prompt: At a high level, how do Snowflake, dbt, and Airflow typically fit together in a single analytics pipeline? Walk through the data's path from a source system to a finished report.
questions.modelAnswer: Each tool owns a distinct stage. Airflow is the orchestrator -- it's typically the thing that kicks off the pipeline on a schedule, triggers an extraction/loading step that pulls raw data from source systems into Snowflake's raw tables (often via a separate loading tool or script that Airflow calls as a task), and then, once that load genuinely completes successfully, triggers dbt to run. Snowflake is where the data actually lives and where all the real computation happens -- both the raw loaded data and every transformed table dbt builds sit inside Snowflake, and dbt's own transformations execute as SQL running inside Snowflake's compute, not somewhere else. dbt is the transformation layer -- it takes the raw tables Airflow's extraction step just loaded and builds the staging, intermediate, and marts models on top of them, entirely as SQL executed against Snowflake, with dbt test run afterward to confirm the output is trustworthy before anyone sees it. Finally, a BI tool like Power BI connects to the finished marts tables and is the thing an actual business user looks at. The overall shape is: Airflow orchestrates the sequence and timing, Snowflake stores the data and performs the computation, dbt defines what transformation happens, and a BI tool presents the end result.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk it in the actual order the data moves. Airflow kicks the whole thing off on a schedule, usually first triggering a task that extracts data from a source system and loads it into Snowflake's raw tables. Once that load task reports success -- not just 'ran', but actually succeeded -- Airflow triggers a second task that runs dbt. dbt then runs entirely as SQL against Snowflake: it builds staging models on the raw tables, intermediate models on top of those, and marts on top of that, and runs its own tests at the end to make sure nothing's obviously broken before anyone relies on it. All of that computation is happening inside Snowflake's compute the whole time -- dbt is generating and sequencing the SQL, Snowflake is the thing actually running it. Once the marts tables are built and tested, a BI tool like Power BI connects to them and that's what a business user actually opens. So the roles are clean: Airflow handles when and in what order things happen, Snowflake handles where the data lives and the actual computation, dbt handles what transformation happens, and the BI tool handles how a person actually sees it.
commonMistakes: Thinking dbt or Airflow perform computation on their own machines instead of generating/orchestrating work that Snowflake actually executes
Running dbt before confirming the raw data load genuinely succeeded, risking transforming incomplete data
Conflating orchestration (Airflow, when/in what order) with transformation (dbt, what logic runs)
Forgetting the BI tool is a separate, final layer connecting only to the finished marts, not to raw or intermediate tables
keyPoints: Airflow orchestrates timing and sequencing (extract/load, then trigger dbt only after success)
Snowflake stores all the data and performs all the actual computation
dbt defines and sequences the SQL transformations (staging -> intermediate -> marts) that run inside Snowflake
A BI tool connects only to the finished marts layer, as the final presentation step

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes each tool's distinct role
Correctly sequences the end-to-end data path
Clarity of the overall explanation

questions.title: Why a dbt source always points at raw, unmodified data
questions.prompt: In dbt, a source is supposed to point at raw, unmodified data exactly as it was loaded -- never at a table that's already been cleaned or transformed. Why does that rule matter architecturally?
questions.modelAnswer: sources.yml is meant to represent a single, clear boundary in the project: everything on the other side of it is raw data that dbt did not create and has no control over, loaded by some external process (an extraction tool, Airflow, a manual load). Everything on this side of that boundary -- every staging, intermediate, and marts model -- is something dbt built and owns, with a traceable lineage back to a source. If a source were allowed to point at an already-transformed table instead of genuinely raw data, that boundary would blur: it would become unclear, just by looking at the project, which tables are truly raw inputs versus which are dbt's own output being disguised as an input, and the dependency graph dbt builds from ref()/source() calls would no longer accurately represent where transformation logic actually lives. Keeping sources strictly raw also makes source freshness checks meaningful -- dbt can check how recently a source's raw data was loaded and warn if it's stale, which only makes sense if a source genuinely represents the most upstream point data entered the warehouse, not some already-processed midpoint.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it as keeping one clear line in the sand: anything declared as a source is raw, external, not something dbt built -- and anything dbt actually builds, no matter how early in the pipeline, goes through ref(), not source(). If I let a source point at something already transformed, that line disappears, and six months later nobody looking at the project can tell at a glance which tables are genuinely raw inputs versus dbt's own earlier output being treated as if it were an input. That matters for understanding the project, but it also matters for a very concrete feature -- source freshness checks, which tell me how recently a source's data was actually loaded. That check only means something if a source genuinely represents the earliest point data entered the warehouse; if it's secretly pointing at something dbt already processed, a freshness check on it is measuring the wrong thing entirely.
commonMistakes: Pointing a source at an already-transformed table instead of using ref() for anything dbt built itself
Blurring the raw/transformed boundary, making the project's actual data lineage unclear
Not realizing source freshness checks only make sense when sources genuinely represent the earliest load point
Treating source() and ref() as interchangeable instead of a deliberate raw-vs-dbt-built distinction
keyPoints: sources.yml marks a strict boundary: raw, externally-loaded data only, never something dbt already transformed
ref() is used for anything dbt itself built, no matter how early in the pipeline
Blurring that boundary makes the project's actual data lineage unclear
Source freshness checks only make sense when a source genuinely represents the earliest load point

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the raw/transformed boundary sources.yml is meant to represent
Correctly distinguishes when source() vs. ref() should be used
Connects the rule to a concrete consequence (freshness checks or lineage clarity)

questions.title: Why put a dbt project under version control instead of a shared drive
questions.prompt: An analytics team currently keeps their SQL transformation scripts (and now, their dbt project) in a shared network folder, with filenames like orders_model_v3_final.sql to track changes. Why would you recommend moving that project into Git instead?
questions.modelAnswer: A shared folder with manually-versioned filenames has no real history -- it only ever shows the latest named version, with no reliable record of exactly what changed between orders_model_v2 and orders_model_v3_final, who made the change, or why. It also has no safe way for two people to work on different changes to the same project at the same time without one directly overwriting the other's in-progress edits, and no way to try something experimental without risking the one copy everyone else depends on. Git solves all three: every commit captures exactly what changed, who changed it, and (via the commit message) why; branches let two people work on separate changes simultaneously without colliding, merging them together deliberately once both are ready; and a bad change can be reverted to any earlier exact state instead of hoping someone kept a backup copy under yet another filename. For a dbt project specifically, Git also becomes the foundation for CI -- running dbt test automatically against a proposed change before it's merged -- which has no equivalent at all for a folder of manually-named files on a shared drive.
questions.professionalAnswer: The 'v3_final' filename is the tell -- that's someone doing version control by hand, badly, because there's no real alternative without an actual tool for it. With a shared folder, I have no genuine history: I can't see exactly what changed between v2 and v3, who changed it, or why, and if two people touch the project at the same time, one of them is probably about to silently overwrite the other's work. Git fixes all of that -- every commit is an exact, timestamped record of what changed and why, branches let two people work on separate things at once without stepping on each other, and reverting a bad change is a real, reliable operation instead of hoping someone still has an old copy saved somewhere. For a dbt project specifically, I'd also point out that Git is what makes CI possible at all -- running dbt test automatically on every proposed change before it's merged, which a shared folder full of hand-named files has no way to do.
commonMistakes: Treating manually-incremented filenames (v2, v3_final) as an adequate substitute for real version control
Not recognizing the collision risk when two people edit the same shared-folder file at the same time
Missing that Git is also the foundation CI (automated testing on every change) depends on
Assuming moving to Git is just a storage-location change rather than a real capability upgrade
keyPoints: Manually-named file versions have no real history of what changed, by whom, or why
A shared folder has no safe way for two people to work on separate changes simultaneously
Git provides real commit history, branching, and reliable reverts
Git is the foundation that makes automated CI testing on a dbt project possible at all

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the real-history and collision problems with the shared-folder approach
Correctly explains what Git provides instead (commits, branches, reverts)
Mentions the CI/testing foundation Git enables
